title: Bananas (per lb)

drivers.name: Price increase (1.5%)
drivers.evidence: One past week at $0.68 (2026-10-05) sold 11.5% below baseline. Noise-adjusted estimate shrinks this to ~5% decline. No other price lifts seen.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 438.2. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price increased 1.5% to $0.68, which is above regular. Historical data shows a consistent 2.5–3.0% sales decline at similar price points (e.g., 2026-09-28: $0.68 → 524 vs 438.2 baseline, but that week had no price lift; 2026-10-05: $0.68 → 388, down 11.5% vs baseline). The heatwave (38°C) may increase demand, but bananas are sensitive to temperature and spoilage risk; past heatwaves show no uplift, only slight shelf-life reduction. The price increase is the only clear driver. Evidence from one comparable week (2026-10-05) shows a 11.5% drop. Adjusting for noise and low signal, apply a 5% downside. Confidence is medium due to sparse evidence.

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 438.2 | 5%-95%: 312.7 - 555.9 | 10%-90%: 346.6 - 529.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-21% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
